name: Lorcaserin (Belviq)

lead: Lorcaserin (Belviq) was a prescription pill for chronic weight management, approved in the US in 2012. It was taken to eat less and lose weight, working toward a leaner look.

It activates serotonin 5-HT2C receptors in the hypothalamus, thought to increase feelings of fullness. In placebo-controlled trials of nearly 8,000 participants it produced roughly 3 to 3.7 percent more weight loss than placebo over up to a year, with diet and exercise counseling.

paras: It was prescribed as a daily pill alongside diet and exercise counseling. It is no longer marketed in the US, so it is discussed as a past weight-loss option.

In 2020 the FDA requested withdrawal after a large safety trial (CAMELLIA-TIMI 61) found more cancer diagnoses among users than on placebo. Doses above the approved range have produced hallucinogenic effects, and the DEA classified it as Schedule IV.

angle.text: Lorcaserin activated serotonin 5-HT2C receptors to increase fullness and reduce eating, leading to weight loss and a leaner look. Trials showed modest weight loss compared with placebo, and it was withdrawn in 2020 over a cancer signal.

lead: Lorcaserin, sold as Belviq, is a selective serotonin 5-HT2C receptor agonist that was prescribed for chronic weight management. It was developed by Arena Pharmaceuticals and approved by the US FDA in 2012. [1][2]

In placebo-controlled trials of nearly 8,000 participants it produced an average weight loss of roughly 3 to 3.7 percent more than placebo over up to a year, alongside diet and exercise counseling. [2] In February 2020 the FDA asked the manufacturer to withdraw it after a large safety trial found more cancer diagnoses among people taking it than on placebo, and approval was withdrawn in September 2020. [2]
No community material tying lorcaserin to appearance or looksmaxxing was identified; this article describes its medical record.

paras: Lorcaserin was approved for adults with a body mass index of 30 or higher, or 27 or higher with a weight-related condition, as an adjunct to diet and exercise. [2] An extended-release version was approved in July 2016. [2] Obesity treatment guidelines and reviews published in this period described it among the available weight-loss medications. [3][4][5]

Three placebo-controlled trials (BLOOM, BLOSSOM and BLOOM-DM) tested lorcaserin in overweight or obese adults, with and without type 2 diabetes. [2][6][7][8] In people without diabetes, about 47 percent lost at least 5 percent of body weight versus about 23 percent on placebo; in people with type 2 diabetes the figures were 38 percent versus 16 percent. [2]
A JAMA systematic review and meta-analysis comparing obesity drugs, and an earlier JAMA review of long-term obesity drug treatment, placed its effect among the more modest in the class. [9][10]

Because the earlier weight-loss drug fenfluramine caused heart valve disease through serotonin 5-HT2B receptors, valve safety was a focus. A 2016 phase 3 trial found valvulopathy in 2.4 percent of lorcaserin users and 2.0 percent of controls, a difference that was not statistically significant. [2]

The CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 trial (about 12,000 participants, five years) found no difference in major adverse cardiovascular events, but more people on lorcaserin were diagnosed with cancer. The trial was designed to measure cardiovascular outcomes rather than cancer. [2] At doses above the approved range, hallucinogenic effects have been reported, attributed to activity at 5-HT2A receptors. [2]

Lorcaserin activates 5-HT2C receptors in the hypothalamus, thought to stimulate POMC neurons and promote satiety. Laboratory characterization reported selectivity for 5-HT2C over 5-HT2A and 5-HT2B (about 17-fold and 100-fold, respectively). [2][11]

Arena Pharmaceuticals submitted a New Drug Application in December 2009. An FDA advisory panel voted 9 to 5 against approval in September 2010 and the FDA declined to approve it in October 2010, citing cancer concerns and marginal efficacy. After further studies the FDA approved it on 27 June 2012. [2]

The DEA classified it as a Schedule IV controlled substance in May 2013. [2] In February 2020 the FDA requested voluntary withdrawal because of the cancer finding; Eisai withdrew it, and FDA withdrew approval in September 2020. [2]

Registered trials have examined lorcaserin for smoking cessation, drug-resistant epilepsy, and chemotherapy-induced neuropathy, although the neuropathy trial was withdrawn and an extended-access epilepsy program is no longer available. [12][13][14]

The BLOOM, BLOSSOM and BLOOM-DM trials tested weight loss over one year or longer in adults with obesity or overweight. [6][7][8] Pharmacokinetic studies were registered in older adults, people with hepatic impairment, adolescents with obesity, and Japanese and Korean volunteers. [15][16][17][18] A real-world clinic study and a trial of predictors of response were also registered. [19][20] A phase 2 trial tested lorcaserin with nicotine patch for smoking cessation. [12]
